title: Smoothness within and across Wardrop route regimes
shortTitle: When a new route opens without a kink
oneLine: Answers to two open questions of Cominetti, Dose and Scarsini on selfish traffic routing: equilibrium link flows stay smooth while the set of cheapest routes is fixed, even for standard BPR costs, but a new route can switch on with no visible kink in total travel time or the price of anarchy; five links are the minimum for this with a common BPR exponent, and such hidden switches are exceptional.
abstract: In a static traffic assignment every traveller uses a cheapest route (Wardrop equilibrium), and the price of anarchy compares the resulting total travel time with the best achievable. Cominetti, Dose and Scarsini (Transportation Research Part B 182, 102922, 2024; arXiv:2305.03459) studied how these quantities change as demand is scaled and left two questions open. First, while the set of cheapest routes stays fixed, are equilibrium link flows continuously differentiable when link costs have zero slope at zero load, as standard BPR costs do? This paper proves that they are, at every interior demand level and on any network; a general version fails at zero demand, and the BPR case there remains open. Second, must the slope of total travel time and of the price of anarchy jump when a new route becomes cheapest, for convex or BPR costs? It need not. A five-link network with ordinary quartic BPR costs has a genuine new route at which total travel time and the price of anarchy have four continuous derivatives; five links are the fewest possible with a common BPR exponent, and larger networks hide any finite number of derivatives. The slope never jumps the wrong way for BPR costs, even with zero free-flow times, and for almost every choice of free-flow times it jumps strictly at nondegenerate breakpoints, so hidden switches are exceptional. When they occur the new route carries flow far below ordinary assignment tolerance; link flows reveal the change earlier than totals. An exploratory Sioux Falls scan finds only transverse activations with visible kinks. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Question 1, yes at interior points: if every link cost is C¹ with positive slope at positive load (BPR costs included), equilibrium link flows are C¹ in demand on every open interval with a fixed set of cheapest routes, on any network (Theorem 3.1, proof). A general extension to zero demand fails (Proposition 3.3, proof); the BPR case there is open.

Question 2, no: a five-link network with common quartic BPR costs has a genuine expansion of the cheapest-route set at which total cost E and the price of anarchy P are C⁴ but not C⁵ (§5.2, proof; exact). Three links suffice with strictly convex or mixed-exponent costs (§5.1).

Five links are the minimum for a common BPR exponent, for expansions and contractions (Theorem 6.1, proof; finite enumeration as a check); m + 2 links give E, P ∈ C^(2m−2) but not C^(2m−1) for every p > 1 (Theorem 5.3, proof).

The slope never jumps the wrong way for BPR costs, even with zero free-flow times (Theorem 4.1, proof), and jumps strictly for almost every free-flow vector at nondegenerate nested breakpoints (Theorem 4.5, proof): hidden switches are exceptional.

Practice: after a hidden switch the new route carries about 0.01% of its commodity after 10% more demand, below ordinary assignment tolerance; link flows reveal the change two derivative orders earlier than totals (numerical). A Sioux Falls scan finds only transverse activations with visible kinks (exploratory).

narration: When a new route opens without a kink. An Evidence Press briefing. When traffic planners model a road network, they usually assume that every driver takes a cheapest route, given everyone else's choices. This is called a Wardrop equilibrium. It is selfish routing, and it can waste time compared with the best possible plan. The ratio between the two is called the price of anarchy. Planners track total travel time and the price of anarchy as demand grows, because they show when congestion starts to bite. As demand grows, new routes become worth using from time to time. In 2024, Cominetti, Dose and Scarsini proved that at such a moment the slope of these curves moves in a predictable direction, and asked two questions. First, while the set of cheapest routes stays the same, do traffic flows change smoothly with demand, even for the standard road-delay formulas that are flat when a road is empty? This paper shows that they do, on any network, except possibly at zero demand. Second, must the curves show a kink when a new route switches on? The answer is no. A network of just five links, with the standard quartic delay formula, has a new route that switches on with no visible trace: total travel time keeps four continuous derivatives. The trick is two parallel groups of roads whose delay curves touch very closely at the switching point. Five links are the fewest possible, and bigger networks can hide the switch even better. But such hidden switches are exceptional. The slope never jumps the wrong way, and for almost every choice of road free-flow times it does jump. For practice, a hidden switch moves only a tiny trickle of traffic, far below the accuracy of a typical assignment run, so watching individual link flows reveals it sooner than watching totals. A test on the Sioux Falls network found only ordinary, visible kinks. This is an anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate, not peer reviewed or independently reproduced. Published on 22 October 2026, its paper and evidence are linked from the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.

decisionObject.description: Answers to the two open questions of Cominetti, Dose and Scarsini (2024): fixed-regime C¹ link flows for costs with zero slope only at zero load, and smooth route-set changes for convex and BPR costs, with a five-link minimal BPR example, a minimality theorem, a weak slope comparison, a genericity theorem and practice-oriented numerics.
decisionObject.scope: Static deterministic multi-commodity Wardrop equilibrium with separable link costs and demands scaled along a path; minimality only for costs a + b z^p with a, b > 0, one common p > 1, all simple paths, proportional positive demands and nested breakpoints; genericity only at nondegenerate breakpoints; no data analysed beyond an exploratory scan of one public test network.
